titulo: Simulado 5 — CCAR-F, simulado final (60 questões · 120 min · 4 cenários)

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. You work at a reinsurance company whose engineers use Claude Code to speed up development of the treaty-pricing and claims platforms: code generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation. The team integrates it into daily work through custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configuration and clear rules for when to use plan mode or direct execution. A production log shows "Retrocession limit exceeded for treaty TR-88412 (layer 3)", and a developer asks Claude to find where this error is raised. The solution has about 2,300 C# files, and the treaty ID and layer number are interpolated at runtime. A teammate proposes that Claude run Glob for **/*Retrocession*.cs and then Read every matching file until it finds the throw site. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: the matching file names narrow the search to the retrocession module, and reading those files gives Claude the surrounding context it needs to explain the error.
Accept it with a change: Glob for **/*Exception*.cs instead, because custom exception classes in a C# solution usually hold the message templates for the errors they raise.
Reject it: have Claude Read the controller that handles treaty requests and follow its calls inward until it reaches the validation code that raises the error.
Reject it: have Claude Grep the solution for a static fragment of the message, such as "limit exceeded for treaty", and then Read only the files that match.
questoes.explicacao: Finding where an error message comes from is a content search, so Grep is the right tool: it searches file contents across the codebase, and searching for the static part of the message avoids the interpolated values. Glob only matches file paths, and the code that raises the message may live in a shared validator whose name has nothing to do with retrocession. Reading only the matching files afterward keeps the investigation incremental.
feedbacks: Tempting because the file names look relevant, but Glob matches paths, not contents. The message can be raised by a shared validator or resource file with an unrelated name, and reading every match is slower than searching for the text itself.
Still a guess based on file names. It assumes a convention for where messages live; Grep finds the text wherever it is, however the files are named.

Tracing from an entry point is a good way to understand a flow, but here you already have a distinctive string. Following calls by hand reads far more code than one content search and can miss paths that do not start at that controller.
Correct. Grep searches file contents, and the static fragment of the interpolated message leads straight to the throw site; Read then loads only the files that matter.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team uses Claude Code for debugging and refactoring. This week a developer is running two long investigations in the same repository: one into a cession-rounding discrepancy and one into slow bordereau imports. Each morning she reopens whichever session was most recent, and twice she landed in the wrong investigation and had to re-explain a day of findings. Nothing in the code has changed since the investigations started. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Start a fresh session for each investigation each morning and paste in a summary of the previous day's findings, so neither depends on being the most recent session.
Use fork_session at the start of each day to branch the most recent session into the investigation she wants, so that each line of work gets its own branch.
Write each day's findings for both investigations into the project CLAUDE.md, so that whichever session she opens next will load them automatically.
Give each investigation its own session name and continue it with --resume <session-name>, so she reopens that exact conversation whatever ran after it.
questoes.explicacao: Named sessions let a developer return to a specific prior conversation with --resume <session-name>, which is exactly what she needs when two investigations alternate. Because the code has not changed, the earlier tool results are still valid, so resuming keeps the full context instead of a lossy summary. The problem is picking the right conversation, not the age of the context.
feedbacks: Starting fresh with an injected summary is the right move when prior tool results are stale. Here the code is unchanged, so she would discard valid context and every detail the summary leaves out.
fork_session creates a divergent branch from a shared baseline. Forking the most recent session would branch the wrong investigation; it does not select the conversation she wants.
CLAUDE.md holds shared project instructions that load in every session for the whole team. Daily investigation notes would pollute it, and it would not reopen either conversation.
Correct. Naming each session and resuming it by name with --resume reopens the specific conversation, with its still-valid context.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team configures Claude Code for its .NET solution. Conventions for EF Core migration files (naming, idempotent scripts, no data changes inside schema migrations) live in src/Claims/CLAUDE.md. Migrations also exist under src/Treaty/Migrations, src/Billing/Data/Migrations and two other modules, and a new module is added every few months. Claude follows the conventions only when it edits migrations in the Claims module. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Move the conventions into .claude/rules/migrations.md with paths: ["**/Migrations/**/*.cs"] in its YAML frontmatter, so they load whenever Claude edits a migration in any module.
Keep the conventions in a shared docs/migrations.md file and add an @import of it to the CLAUDE.md of each module that contains migrations, so the modules share one source.
Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md under a "Migrations" heading, so they are loaded in every session and Claude can apply them to any migration it edits.
Package the conventions as a project skill in .claude/skills/ and ask developers to invoke it before they write a migration, so the conventions are applied on demand.
questoes.explicacao: Migration files are spread across several modules, and new modules keep appearing. A .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob loads the conventions whenever Claude edits a matching file, regardless of its directory, so new modules are covered automatically. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files, with or without @import, cover only the directories someone remembered to configure.
feedbacks: Correct. A path-scoped rule matches migrations by pattern wherever they live and loads only when such files are being edited.
@import removes duplication, but it still depends on a CLAUDE.md in each module directory. A new module with migrations gets no conventions until someone adds the import.

This makes the conventions available, but they would load in every session, including work that never touches migrations, and Claude would have to infer when the section applies. A path-scoped rule targets exactly the files that need it.
Skills are invoked on demand. Conventions that must apply every time a migration is edited should not depend on a developer remembering to invoke something.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team uses Claude Code to understand a legacy claims-reserving engine. Early in a long exploration session, Claude read ReserveFactorCalculator and reported that it rounds each development period to four decimals. Two hours later, asked how reserve factors are rounded, it answers that "reserving engines typically round only the final reserve" and names no class. The team is deciding how to run the remaining weeks of exploration. Which approach best addresses what happened?
opcoes: Treat it as context degradation in a long session: have Claude record every confirmed finding, with class names, in a scratchpad file and consult that file for later questions.
Treat it as missing domain knowledge: add a reserving glossary and the engine's design notes to the project CLAUDE.md, so later answers stay anchored in this codebase.
Treat it as a correction of the earlier analysis: ask the rounding question again in a fresh session and keep whichever answer that fresh session gives.
Treat it as a limit of the context window: switch to a model with a larger context window, so that the earlier reading of the calculator stays available.
questoes.explicacao: Inconsistent answers that fall back on "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes found earlier are the signature of context degradation in extended sessions. Recording confirmed findings in a scratchpad file and consulting it for later questions keeps those facts available across context boundaries. The earlier finding came from reading the actual class, so the generic answer is the regression, not the correction.
feedbacks: Correct. A scratchpad of confirmed findings counters context degradation by keeping specific facts outside the fading conversation.
Background documentation helps orientation, but Claude had already found the specific behavior in this codebase. The finding faded during a long session; domain knowledge was not what was missing.
The earlier answer was grounded in reading the class, and the later one cites no class at all. A fresh session could give either answer, and nothing prevents the same degradation later.
A larger window does not stop attention to early details from degrading as verbose output accumulates. Persisting findings outside the conversation is the reliable fix.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team uses Claude Code with MCP servers. A developer prototyped an MCP server for the internal treaty catalog and registered it in her ~/.claude.json, next to a personal server that queries her own scratch database. The team now wants the treaty-catalog server available to everyone who clones the repository, while the scratch-database server stays personal. What should you change?
opcoes: Commit a copy of her ~/.claude.json to the repository's docs folder and ask each developer to merge the treaty-catalog entry into their own user configuration.
Move both server definitions into the project .mcp.json, so the team's whole MCP configuration lives in one version-controlled file that is easy to review.
Describe the treaty-catalog server's command and arguments in the project CLAUDE.md, so that Claude Code can start the server for anyone who opens the repository.
Move only the treaty-catalog entry into the project .mcp.json, with its token as ${TREATY_CATALOG_TOKEN}, and keep the scratch server in her ~/.claude.json.
questoes.explicacao: The project-scoped .mcp.json is version-controlled and shared with everyone who clones the repository, which is where shared team tooling belongs; the user-scoped ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers. Environment variable expansion keeps the credential out of the committed file.
feedbacks: This pushes manual setup onto every developer and lets configurations drift. The project .mcp.json shares the server automatically through version control.
One file is tidy, but it would push her personal scratch-database server onto the whole team. Experimental servers belong in user scope.
CLAUDE.md provides instructions and context, not MCP server configuration. Claude Code discovers servers from the MCP configuration files, not from prose.
Correct. Shared tooling goes in the project .mcp.json with ${VAR} expansion for the token; the personal server stays in user scope.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team shares Claude Code commands through its repository. A lead created a /bordereau-check command that validates parser changes, tested it and announced it in the team channel. Teammates who pulled the latest main say the command does not exist, although they use /release-notes, which lives in the repository's .claude/commands/ directory, every day. When the lead ran git status after creating the command, there was nothing new to commit. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The teammates' sessions were started before they pulled, and slash commands are discovered when a session starts, so they need to restart Claude Code to see it.
The lead saved bordereau-check.md in her personal ~/.claude/commands/ directory, so the file never became part of the repository that her teammates pulled.
The command file has no description in its frontmatter, so Claude Code does not list it in the slash-command menu for developers other than its author.
The repository's .gitignore excludes files under .claude/, so the command file was left out of the lead's last push along with her other local configuration.
questoes.explicacao: Two details point to where the file was saved: git status showed nothing to commit, and the team's other project command in .claude/commands/ reaches everyone, which rules out an ignored directory. A command saved in ~/.claude/commands/ is personal and works only for its author; to share it, it must be committed under the repository's .claude/commands/.
feedbacks: Restarting matters only if the file is in the repository. A clean git status right after creating the command means it never entered the repository.
Correct. User-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are personal; team commands must be committed under the project's .claude/commands/.
Project commands have no per-author visibility rule. A command in the repository's .claude/commands/ is available to everyone who has the repository.
This would also explain the clean git status, but /release-notes lives in the same .claude/commands/ directory and reaches every teammate, so that directory is not being ignored.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team uses Claude Code for a two-phase refactoring of its premium-allocation service. In phase 1, a 90-minute session mapped how premium data flows through the service and found a regulator-mandated rounding rule that every change must keep. In phase 2, Claude spawned three subagents to draft refactoring proposals for different modules. Each spent about 20 minutes rediscovering the data flow, and one proposed removing the mandated rounding. Which TWO changes should you make before the next phase? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Before the phase starts, have Claude condense the phase-1 findings into a short summary of entry points, data flow and constraints.
Attach the full phase-1 transcript to each subagent, so that each subagent can see each file and each finding from the earlier exploration.
Run the next phase in the main session without subagents, so the drafts are written with the whole phase-1 conversation still in context.
Tell each subagent to begin by re-exploring the service with Grep and Read, so its proposal rests on its own first-hand analysis of the code.
Include the key phase-1 findings in each subagent's initial prompt, since subagents do not see the main session's conversation unless it is passed.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents start without the main session's history, so findings from an earlier phase must be passed to them explicitly. Summarizing the key findings first and then injecting that summary into each subagent's initial context gives every subagent the data flow and the non-negotiable constraint, without repeating the exploration or flooding its context with verbose discovery output.
feedbacks: Correct. Summarizing the phase's key findings is the first half of the pattern.
The transcript contains the findings, but it also carries 90 minutes of verbose discovery output into each subagent's context, which is what delegation is meant to avoid.
Keeping everything in one session avoids passing context, but the main session is already full of verbose discovery output and would degrade further while drafting three proposals.
This is what happened in the failed run: each subagent repeated the exploration, and one still missed the rounding constraint.
Correct. Passing the key findings explicitly in each subagent's initial prompt makes the constraints part of its context from the start.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team uses Claude Code to generate code for its loss-triangle module. After generating a new development-factor calculator, a developer asks the same session to "review your code carefully for bugs". This happened on two features, and both times the review passed and QA later found an off-by-one error in the development-period indexing. Which TWO changes would most improve the detection of issues like this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Enable extended thinking for the review request in the same session, so the model reasons longer and more explicitly about the code it generated.
Extend the review prompt in the same session with explicit instructions to question each assumption and re-derive each index boundary step by step.
Add a CI step that runs a fresh Claude Code review with -p on every pull request, using the review criteria documented in the project CLAUDE.md.
Run the review in a new Claude Code session that receives only the diff and the requirements, without the conversation that produced the code.
Run /compact before asking the same session to review, so the review starts from a condensed summary rather than from the full generation history.
questoes.explicacao: The session that generated the code keeps its own reasoning context and is unlikely to question its earlier decisions, so stronger self-review instructions, longer reasoning or a compacted history do not remove the bias. An independent instance that sees only the diff and the specification reviews the code on its own terms, whether it is started by hand or as an automated CI step.
feedbacks: Independent review instances catch subtle issues more effectively than extended thinking in the generating session; more reasoning in the same context tends to confirm the original decisions.
Stronger self-review instructions still run inside the context that produced the code, which is the source of the blind spot.
Correct. A CI review run with -p is a fresh instance without the generation context, and CLAUDE.md supplies the review criteria.
Correct. A separate session without the generator's reasoning context reviews the code independently.
/compact replaces the history with a summary of it, and that summary still carries the generator's decisions and rationale. The reviewer is still the author.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team is removing a deprecated internal library, Legacy.Actuarial.Math, from a solution of about 2,300 C# files. A developer asks Claude Code for every file that still imports its namespace. A teammate proposes that Claude run Glob for **/*Actuarial*.cs and Read each match, because the team names files after the domain they work with. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: the naming convention makes Glob a precise filter, and reading each match also shows how the library is used, which the removal plan will need.
Accept it with a refinement: first Read the .csproj files that reference the library, then Read all the source files in those projects to find the usages.
Reject it: have Claude Grep the source files for the using Legacy.Actuarial.Math directive and qualified references, since imports are file contents.
Reject it: have Claude Glob for **/*.cs and Read each file in batches, since only a full read of the solution is sure to catch each reference to the namespace.
questoes.explicacao: Finding which files import a namespace is a content search: the using directive is text inside the files, not part of their names. Grep finds every import and fully qualified reference however the files are named, while Glob matches only paths and depends on a convention that may not hold. Reading files up front wastes context when one search answers the question.
feedbacks: A naming convention is not a guarantee: any file that imports the namespace without the domain in its name would be missed. Imports are content, which is what Grep searches.
Narrowing to projects is reasonable, but reading every file in them costs far more than one content search for text that Grep finds directly.
Correct. Grep searches file contents, so it finds the using directives and qualified references regardless of file names.
A full read would find the references, but at a huge context cost. Grep searches all file contents without loading them into the conversation.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team decides task by task whether Claude Code should work in plan mode or with direct execution, and the tech lead wants plan mode reserved for work where it prevents rework. This week's backlog includes the tasks below. Which TWO of these tasks are best handled with direct execution? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a check to TreatyValidator.Validate that rejects a treaty whose inception date falls after its expiry date, returning the existing validation error type.
Add a facultative contract type that pricing, accounting and reporting must all support; two engineers have proposed competing data models for it.
Fix a NullReferenceException in CedentStatementParser.ParseHeader; the stack trace points to line 87, where Header is null for statements with no header row.
Fix premiums that sometimes differ by one cent between the pricing API and the nightly report; nobody yet knows which of three rounding paths is responsible.
Replace the hand-written XML serializer in the bordereau import modules with System.Text.Json; 38 files are affected, several of them with custom converters.
questoes.explicacao: Direct execution fits well-understood changes with a clear scope: a single-file bug fix whose stack trace pinpoints the failure, or one validation conditional in a known method. The other tasks involve an unknown cause spread over several code paths, a library migration across many files, or an architectural choice between competing designs, which is what plan mode is for.
feedbacks: Correct. A single date-validation conditional in a known method is a well-scoped change.
Competing data models across three modules is an architectural decision, the textbook case for plan mode.
Correct. The stack trace identifies the file, the line and the condition, so the scope is clear.
It looks like a small fix, but the cause is unknown and could sit in any of three code paths. Exploring before changing code avoids fixing the wrong path.
A library migration across 38 files with custom converters is a multi-file change with design decisions; planning first prevents costly rework.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team uses Claude Code on its pricing platform. It must integrate a new catastrophe-model vendor and has two options: call the vendor's API synchronously from the pricing service, or ingest the vendor's nightly files through the existing ETL pipeline. The options need different infrastructure, and either one will touch the pricing, exposure-management and reporting modules. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Use plan mode to have Claude explore the affected modules and lay out both integration approaches, with their dependencies and impacts, before any code is changed.
Use direct execution to build the synchronous API client behind an interface, so that the team can switch to file ingestion later if it turns out to be the better fit.
Use direct execution with a detailed prompt that describes the ETL approach step by step, since the nightly pipeline already exists and is the more familiar option.
Use the Explore subagent to list the files that reference exposure data, then switch to direct execution and implement whichever approach touches fewer files.
questoes.explicacao: Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements, across several modules, is an architectural decision. Plan mode lets Claude explore safely and compare the approaches before anything is changed, which prevents costly rework. Once an approach is chosen, the implementation can proceed with direct execution.
feedbacks: Correct. Plan mode is designed for architectural decisions with multiple valid approaches and multi-module impact.
An interface does not make the decision for you: the options differ in infrastructure, not just in client code. Building first risks rework once dependencies surface.
Familiarity is not an analysis. A detailed prompt assumes the decision is already made, without exploring how each option affects the three modules.
Explore helps with discovery, but the number of files touched is not a design criterion. The approaches differ in infrastructure and behavior, which calls for planning, not just a file list.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team is changing how the claims service logs personal data. Phase 1 finds every place that logs personal fields across about 400 files, phase 2 designs a redaction approach and phase 3 implements it. In a first attempt, by the time phase 2 started, the main conversation was full of search hits and file excerpts, and Claude's design ignored two constraints the developer had stated at the start. Which design should the team use for the next attempt?
opcoes: Run phase 1 in the main conversation, then use /compact before phase 2, so the search output is condensed while the work stays in one single session.
Run each phase in a separate session and paste the previous phase's output into the next one, so no session accumulates more than one phase of output.
Delegate phase 1 to the Explore subagent, so the verbose search output stays in its own context and only a summary of locations and patterns returns.
Limit phase 1 to reading only the first 50 lines of each file, so the discovery output stays small enough to leave room for the design discussion.
questoes.explicacao: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output in its own context and returns a summary, so the main conversation keeps the developer's constraints and the design discussion intact. Compacting afterward condenses everything, including the constraints stated at the start, and separate sessions make the developer carry the outputs by hand.
feedbacks: /compact is useful when context fills up, but it summarizes the whole history, including the two constraints that were already being lost. Isolating discovery from the start keeps them intact.
This avoids accumulation but makes the developer transfer context by hand and breaks the continuity of the conversation. The Explore subagent does the isolation and summarizing for you.
Correct. Explore keeps verbose discovery out of the main context and returns only what the design phase needs.
Logging calls can be anywhere in a file, so this makes discovery incomplete. The problem is where the output lands, not how much of each file is read.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team keeps OpenAPI contract files (*.openapi.yaml) next to each service, in 11 directories across the repository. Their conventions (shared error schema, versioned paths, no inline examples) are in contracts/CLAUDE.md, a directory that now holds only two of the files, and Claude ignores the conventions for the other nine. The team also wants these conventions kept out of context when Claude works on anything other than contract files. What should you change?
opcoes: Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md under a "Contracts" heading, so Claude has them in every session and can apply them wherever a contract file lives.
Move the conventions into a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.openapi.yaml"], so they load when Claude edits a contract file, whatever directory it is in.
Copy contracts/CLAUDE.md into each of the 11 service directories that hold a contract file, so the conventions load wherever Claude is editing a contract.
Move all contract files into the contracts/ directory and update the build to read them there, so the existing directory-level CLAUDE.md covers each contract.
questoes.explicacao: A path-scoped rule activates by file pattern rather than by directory, so it covers contract files wherever they live and loads only while one of them is being edited. That meets both requirements: coverage across directories and no extra context for unrelated work. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are bound to their directory, which is why the conventions reached only two files.
feedbacks: This covers every directory but breaks the second requirement: the conventions would load in every session, including work that never touches a contract.
Correct. A glob in the rule's paths frontmatter applies the conventions by file type, regardless of directory, and only when matching files are edited.
Copies would work today, but they must be kept in sync and added for every new service. A glob-based rule covers new locations automatically.
Restructuring the repository to suit the tooling is costly and fights the team's chosen layout. A glob pattern adapts the configuration to the code instead.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team connected Claude Code to an internal MCP server for its treaty data warehouse, which offers two tools: run_query and describe_table. When developers ask Claude to write a report query, logs show it calling describe_table on 15 to 25 guessed table names, several of which do not exist, before it writes any SQL. Each request takes several minutes and fills the context with table descriptions. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The server exposes no catalog of the available tables and schemas as an MCP resource, so Claude can only learn what exists through exploratory calls.
The describe_table tool's description lacks example inputs and edge cases, so Claude cannot tell when it should call describe_table rather than run_query.
Claude Code loads tools from each configured MCP server at once, and overlap between the servers leads Claude to probe several of them before writing a query.
The run_query tool reports failures without the isError flag, so Claude cannot tell a failed query from an empty result and keeps probing tables to be safe.
questoes.explicacao: Claude is calling describe_table to discover what exists, guessing names along the way. Exposing a content catalog, such as the list of tables with their schemas, as an MCP resource gives the agent visibility into the available data without exploratory tool calls. Descriptions and error signaling matter, but the logs show discovery behavior, not misrouting or failed queries.
feedbacks: Correct. MCP resources expose content catalogs such as database schemas, which removes the need for exploratory calls.
Claude is choosing describe_table appropriately for the step it is on; the problem is that it has to guess which tables exist. A better description does not tell it what the warehouse contains.
Tools from all servers are available at the same time, but the logs show repeated calls to one server's describe_table with guessed names, not probing across servers.
Clear error signaling matters, but the probing happens before any SQL is written, so failed queries cannot be what drives it.

questoes.pergunta: Your reinsurance team built a Claude Code review command for large refactoring pull requests. It runs one pass per changed file with the instruction "check for local bugs and cross-module consistency" and concatenates the per-file findings. On a 22-file pull request, the passes caught several local bugs, but a change of the LayerLimit amount from thousands to units in one file broke calculations in three consuming files, and no pass flagged it. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: Per-file passes cannot see the whole pull request, so the review should go back to a single pass over the 22 files, where the model can compare each change.
The per-file prompt is vague about consistency; it needs explicit criteria with examples of unit and contract changes, so each pass knows what to flag.
Single runs are noisy, so the command should run each per-file pass three times and keep only the findings that appear in at least two of the runs.
There is no separate integration pass; cross-file data flow, such as a changed unit and its consumers, needs its own pass over changed interfaces and callers.
questoes.explicacao: Per-file passes give consistent depth on local issues, but a pass that sees one file cannot detect that a change breaks consumers in other files. The fix is to keep the per-file passes and add a separate integration pass focused on cross-file data flow. Going back to a single pass would reintroduce attention dilution.
feedbacks: A single pass over 22 files brings back the attention dilution that per-file passes solve: uneven depth and missed bugs.
Better criteria help each pass judge what it sees, but the consumers are in files that the pass never sees. No prompt gives a per-file pass visibility into them.
Voting across runs suppresses issues that are caught only intermittently, and it does nothing for a problem that no pass can see.
Correct. Per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow is the multi-pass review pattern.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. You work at a retail pharmacy chain that built a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents (one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings and one generates reports), and the system produces comprehensive, cited reports on topics such as drug shortages, pricing and regulation. For a shortage report, the document analysis subagent calls lookup_drug_label for 60 products. Each result has about 45 fields (packaging codes, revision history, manufacturer addresses), but the analysis uses only four: active ingredient, strength, approval date and shortage status. After roughly 35 lookups, its analyses become shallow and later products are skipped. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: The subagent is reaching its max_tokens limit, because each lookup result is echoed back in its response; raising that limit would let it finish all 60 analyses.
Each new tool result replaces the previous one in the subagent's context, so by the later lookups it has lost track of the products and analyzes them superficially.
The label database returns differently shaped results for some products, which the model cannot parse reliably after many lookups, so it skips those products.
The full results pile up in the subagent's context, using tokens out of proportion to the four relevant fields; trimming each result to those fields addresses it.
questoes.explicacao: Tool results are appended to the conversation and stay there, so 60 results of about 45 fields each consume context far out of proportion to the four fields the task needs. Trimming each result to the relevant fields before it accumulates keeps the context focused and leaves room for the remaining analyses.
feedbacks: max_tokens limits the length of a single response. The symptom here is gradual degradation as the input context grows, not truncated output.
Tool results are appended to the conversation history, not replaced, which is exactly why they accumulate.
Nothing in the symptoms points to parsing failures. The degradation tracks the number of lookups, which matches accumulating context.
Correct. Verbose tool results accumulate and crowd the context; keeping only the relevant fields prevents it.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's research system runs its coordinator in an agentic loop. Today the loop ends when the coordinator's latest text contains the word "complete", and in 3% of runs it stops early because the coordinator wrote that "the shortage section is not complete yet". An engineer proposes replacing the word check with a fixed cap of 15 iterations, because most runs finish in 9 to 12. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: a fixed cap is deterministic and bounds the cost of each run, which is more reliable than interpreting the model's own wording to decide when to stop.
Reject it: continue while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stop on "end_turn", keeping an iteration limit only as a safety guard rather than as the stopping rule.
Accept it and keep the word check as well, stopping at whichever comes first, so runs that finish early end promptly and long runs are still bounded.
Reject it: end the loop as soon as a response contains a text block, since the coordinator writes prose only after it has finished calling its subagents.
questoes.explicacao: The loop should be driven by stop_reason: keep executing tools while it is "tool_use" and finish when it is "end_turn". Parsing natural-language signals, using an arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stop and treating text content as a completion signal are all anti-patterns; a cap of 15 would cut off legitimately long research runs. A limit can remain as a safety net.
feedbacks: A cap is deterministic but arbitrary: runs that legitimately need more iterations are cut off mid-research, and reaching it says nothing about whether the work is done.
Correct. stop_reason is the completion signal; an iteration limit is only a safeguard.
This combines two anti-patterns: the word check still misfires on wording, and the cap is still the primary stop for long runs.
Responses can contain text alongside tool_use blocks, so the presence of text is not a reliable completion indicator; stop_reason is.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's research system runs the same fixed sequence for every request: web search, then document analysis, then synthesis, then the report. For "summarize the attached formulary memo", it still runs six web searches and pads the report with unrelated sources, and when an analysis raises a new question it cannot go back to search. The team must keep the existing subagents and their tools unchanged. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Turn the sequence into a decision tree with branches for the common cases, such as skipping search when documents are attached and repeating search when a gap is found.
Let the coordinator decide in its loop which subagent to call next, reasoning over the request and the results so far, guided by research goals and quality criteria.
Add a classifier in front of the pipeline that assigns each request to one of four predefined pipelines, each a fixed sequence tuned for that type of request.
Keep the sequence but instruct each subagent to return a short "not needed" result when its step does not apply, so that later stages can proceed quickly.
questoes.explicacao: The underlying problem is a pre-configured tool sequence that cannot adapt. With model-driven decision-making, the coordinator reasons over the request and intermediate results to choose the next subagent, so it can skip unnecessary steps and go back when a new question appears, without changing the subagents. Decision trees and fixed pipelines cover only the cases someone anticipated.
feedbacks: Branches handle the cases listed today, but each new kind of request or finding needs another branch. It is still a pre-configured sequence.
Correct. Model-driven orchestration lets the coordinator choose the next step from context instead of following a fixed script.
A classifier adds infrastructure and still ends in fixed sequences, so a finding that raises a new question still cannot redirect the work.
Every stage still runs, and the pipeline still cannot go back to search when a finding raises a new question.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's research system handles two recurring kinds of work. One is a weekly competitor price report that always covers the same five retailers, sections and sources. The other is open-ended investigations, such as why insulin pen refills dropped 18% in the Northeast last quarter. Which TWO statements correctly apply task decomposition patterns to this work? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Use dynamic decomposition for both kinds of work but cap it at three subtasks per run, so that costs stay predictable while the coordinator adapts.
Run the insulin-refill investigation as a fixed chain of search, analysis and synthesis, so that each run follows the same auditable sequence of steps.
In the insulin-refill investigation, let the coordinator create subtasks from intermediate findings, such as a supplier search after a recall turns up.
Keep the weekly price report as a fixed sequential pipeline, since its sections and sources are known in advance and are the same every week.
Run the weekly price report with dynamic decomposition, so the coordinator can decide afresh each week which retailers and sources are worth checking.
questoes.explicacao: Prompt chaining suits predictable, multi-aspect work whose steps are known in advance, like the weekly report. Open-ended investigations need dynamic, adaptive decomposition, in which the plan generates new subtasks from what each step discovers.
feedbacks: An arbitrary cap of three subtasks can stop the investigation before it follows the leads that matter, and the weekly report does not need adaptation at all.
An open-ended investigation cannot know its steps in advance; a fixed chain cannot follow a lead such as a supplier recall.
Correct. Adaptive decomposition generates subtasks from what each step discovers.
Correct. Predictable work with known steps fits a fixed sequential pipeline.
The report's retailers, sections and sources are fixed; re-deciding them each week adds variability without benefit.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain asks its research system to "assess our exposure to generic drug shortages" across a portfolio of about 2,000 generic products. The first run fanned out one search per product and returned 2,000 disconnected snippets that no one could prioritize. The team is comparing designs for the next run. Which approach should the coordinator take?
opcoes: Fan out one search subagent per therapeutic class right away, in parallel, and merge whatever each subagent finds into a single report at the end.
Map the portfolio first (classes, single-source suppliers, sales volume), then prioritize high-impact areas in a plan that adapts as dependencies appear.
Have the coordinator write a complete plan of 40 subtasks before any research starts, so that the run stays predictable and each subtask can be audited.
Have the synthesis subagent draft a report outline first, then send search subagents out to find the evidence for each section of that outline.
questoes.explicacao: Open-ended tasks are best decomposed by first mapping the structure, then identifying high-impact areas, then building a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered, for example when many products turn out to share one ingredient supplier. Fanning out immediately or fixing every subtask up front spreads the work evenly and cannot react to what is found.
feedbacks: Partitioning by class reduces duplication, but without first mapping the portfolio nothing tells you which classes carry the most risk, and nothing adapts when a shared supplier links several classes.
Correct. Map, prioritize by impact, then adapt the plan as dependencies are discovered.
A full plan up front is predictable, but it cannot adapt when the research uncovers dependencies, such as one supplier behind many products.
An outline written before any research biases the work toward expected conclusions and does not prioritize by impact.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's research system pulls wholesale prices from three third-party MCP servers. One returns integer cents, one returns strings such as "$12.40" and one returns decimals in Canadian dollars, while dates arrive as Unix timestamps or ISO 8601. In 5% of reports, the synthesis compares mismatched values. The vendors will not change their servers, and the team needs a guarantee that every value is in USD and ISO 8601 before the model reasons about it. What should you change?
opcoes: Add rules to the analysis subagent's system prompt that require converting each price to USD and each date to ISO 8601 before it compares any values.
Have the report subagent normalize the prices and dates while it formats the final document, so each value in the published report uses one format.
Add a PostToolUse hook on the three vendor tools that converts prices to USD and dates to ISO 8601 before the results reach the model.
Add a PreToolUse hook on the three vendor tools that rewrites each request to ask for USD prices and ISO 8601 dates before the call is sent.
questoes.explicacao: A PostToolUse hook intercepts tool results and transforms them before the model processes them, which gives a deterministic guarantee that every value is normalized, without changing the vendor servers. Prompt rules are probabilistic, and normalizing at the end is too late because the comparisons have already been made.
feedbacks: Prompt instructions lower the error rate but cannot guarantee it, and the requirement is a guarantee.
By the time the report is formatted, the synthesis has already compared mismatched values. Normalization must happen before the model reasons about the data.
Correct. PostToolUse hooks normalize heterogeneous tool results deterministically before the model sees them.
A hook on outgoing calls controls what is requested, not what comes back; it helps only if each vendor supports such options. Transforming results is the job of a PostToolUse hook.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's document analysis subagent must report every result by calling one of two tools, record_findings or record_no_relevant_content, because the coordinator reads the tool_use input. In 6% of runs it replies with prose such as "I reviewed the circular and found...", and the coordinator's parser fails. The request includes both tools and "tool_choice": {"type": "auto"}. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The two tool descriptions are too similar, so when the model cannot decide between them, it falls back to describing its results in a plain text reply.
With tool_choice set to "auto", the model may answer in text instead of calling a tool; "any" would require it to call one of the two tools.
The subagent's max_tokens is too low, so long findings are cut off before the tool call is emitted, and only the prose part of the reply survives.
The system prompt does not state forcefully enough that each reply must be a tool call, so the model sometimes treats that instruction as optional.
questoes.explicacao: tool_choice "auto" lets the model decide whether to call a tool or reply with text, so an occasional text reply is expected behavior, not a malfunction. Setting tool_choice to "any" guarantees that the model calls one of the provided tools while still letting it choose which one. Prompt wording only lowers the rate of text replies.
feedbacks: Overlapping descriptions cause the wrong tool to be chosen, not a text reply in place of a tool call.
Correct. "auto" allows text replies; "any" guarantees a call to one of the tools.
A max_tokens cutoff would show stop_reason "max_tokens" and truncated output, not complete prose replies.
Stronger wording may lower the rate, but the configuration explicitly allows text replies; only tool_choice can guarantee a tool call.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's coordinator runs search, analysis and synthesis, then asks the synthesis subagent to list coverage gaps. If any are listed, the coordinator appends them to the report as a "Limitations" note and finishes. Reports on biosimilar adoption in community pharmacies keep shipping with notes such as "insufficient data on Medicaid reimbursement", although analysts find such sources in minutes. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The coordinator records gaps but never acts on them; it should send targeted queries to search and analysis and re-run synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
The synthesis subagent cannot fill gaps on its own; it should be given web search tools so it can find the missing sources while it writes the synthesis.
The coordinator's initial decomposition is too narrow; it should cover reimbursement from the start, so that the synthesis never needs to report gaps.
The coordinator treats gaps as minor; it should mark any run with reported gaps as failed and re-execute the whole pipeline from the original request.
questoes.explicacao: The point of having the coordinator evaluate synthesis output is an iterative refinement loop: when gaps appear, it re-delegates targeted queries to search and analysis, then re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient. Here the gap list becomes a disclaimer instead of a work queue. A broader initial decomposition helps, but gaps will still appear and must be acted on.
feedbacks: Correct. Evaluate, re-delegate targeted queries, re-synthesize: that is the refinement loop the design is missing.
Giving synthesis full search tools invites cross-specialization misuse; filling gaps should be re-delegated through the coordinator.
Broader decomposition is good practice, but no plan anticipates every gap. The flaw is that detected gaps are never acted on.
Re-running everything is wasteful and untargeted, and the same request will probably reproduce the same gaps.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's report subagent can call publish_report. Policy says reports that cite the licensed prescription-volume dataset may not go to the all-staff portal and must go through request_compliance_review instead. The team added a hook that intercepts publish_report, blocks any call that targets the all-staff portal with such a report, and returns a message saying to use request_compliance_review. In testing, the model then called request_compliance_review. Which statement about this design is correct?
opcoes: The design works only because the model chose to follow the returned message, so a clear system-prompt rule would give the same guarantee with fewer moving parts.
The block holds whatever the model decides, because the hook stops the call before it runs; the returned message then redirects the model to the review workflow.
The hook should run after publish_report executes, so that it can inspect the published report's final content before deciding whether the publication was allowed.
Because the hook blocks violations, the system prompt should stop mentioning the policy, so that the model does not hesitate or second-guess the hook's decisions.
questoes.explicacao: Intercepting the outgoing tool call gives a deterministic guarantee: the violating publication never executes, whatever the model intended. Returning a message that names the alternative workflow lets the model continue productively by requesting compliance review. A prompt rule alone would leave a non-zero chance of a violating publication.
feedbacks: The model's cooperation affects only what happens next; the block itself does not depend on it. A prompt rule cannot guarantee that the violating call never runs.
Correct. Interception enforces the rule before execution, and the redirect keeps the workflow moving.
Inspecting after execution means the report has already reached the wrong audience. Rules about actions must be enforced before the call runs.
The hook guarantees compliance, but prompt guidance still helps the model pick the right route first instead of hitting the block repeatedly.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's document analysis subagent receives 25 pharmacy-benefit-manager contracts at once and is asked to compare their rebate and audit terms. The output is detailed for some contracts and superficial for others, and it labels the same rebate clause "standard" in one contract and "unusual" in another. An engineer proposes analyzing each contract in its own focused call, then running a separate pass that compares the per-contract results. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it: send all 25 contracts in one call to a model with a larger context window, so each contract gets attention and the comparison happens in a single step.
Reject it: run the all-at-once analysis three times and keep only the classifications that at least two of the runs agree on, which removes the contradictions.
Adopt it: per-contract passes give each contract consistent depth, and the separate comparison pass handles the terms that must be compared across contracts.
Adopt the per-contract calls but drop the separate comparison pass, since the per-contract results can be concatenated directly into the analysts' report.
questoes.explicacao: This is prompt chaining: break the work into focused per-item passes, then run a separate integration pass across their results. Each contract gets the same depth, and the cross-contract pass is where terms are compared consistently. A larger window does not fix attention dilution, and voting suppresses findings instead of fixing their cause.
feedbacks: A larger context window holds more text, but it does not give each contract equal attention.
Consensus voting can hide the inconsistency without fixing it, and it may drop correct findings that appear in only one run.
Correct. Per-item passes plus a cross-item integration pass is the chaining pattern for this kind of review.
The task is a comparison. Without the integration pass, nothing reconciles how the same clause is classified across contracts.

questoes.pergunta: Three weeks ago, your pharmacy chain's research team paused a named session that was researching GLP-1 drug supply. Since then, the regulator's shortage list has been updated and two manufacturers have published new supply statements, which together cover most of the sources the session had fetched. The team wants to finish the report this week. What is the most effective way to continue?
opcoes: Resume the named session with --resume, since it already holds the full analysis and each fetched source, and have it complete the report from there.
Use fork_session on the paused session, so the new work runs on a separate branch while the original analysis stays intact for later comparison.
Resume the named session and add a note that some of its data may be out of date, so the agent re-checks whatever it judges to be outdated.
Start a new session with a structured summary of the prior conclusions and their dates, marking which sources must be fetched again before finishing.
questoes.explicacao: Resuming is the right choice when prior context is mostly valid. Here most of the fetched results are stale, so a resumed session would reason from outdated tool results. Starting fresh with a structured summary keeps the conclusions and their dates while making clear which sources must be fetched again.
feedbacks: The session holds the analysis, but it rests on tool results that are now mostly outdated, and the agent would treat them as current.
A fork starts from the same stale baseline, so both branches would still rely on outdated results.
Telling a resumed session about specific changes works when most of its context is still valid. Here most sources changed, and a vague warning leaves the agent guessing which results to trust.
Correct. With stale tool results, a fresh session with an injected structured summary is more reliable than resuming.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's coordinator concatenates the outputs of nine search and analysis subagents, in the order they finish, into a single input for the synthesis subagent. An audit of 50 reports shows that findings from the outputs placed fourth to sixth appear in 22% of reports, against 85% for the first and last outputs. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Randomize the order of the subagent outputs on each run, so that no single subagent's findings sit in the middle of the input every time.
Run a separate synthesis for each of the nine subagent outputs, and concatenate the partial syntheses into the final report that analysts read.
Put a summary of key findings at the start of the input and organize every subagent's detailed results under explicit section headers.
Move the synthesis subagent to a model with a larger context window, so that all nine outputs fit comfortably and get the same attention.
questoes.explicacao: Models reliably use information at the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit findings from the middle. Placing a key-findings summary at the start and organizing the detailed results under explicit headers mitigates this position effect. Randomizing the order only spreads the omissions around.
feedbacks: Randomizing spreads the omissions across subagents instead of reducing them.
Separate syntheses lose the cross-source integration that the synthesis step exists to provide.
Correct. Key findings up front and clear section headers counter the lost-in-the-middle effect.
The outputs already fit in the window; the problem is their position, not capacity.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain is replacing application code that called four agents in a fixed order with a coordinator that delegates on its own. The team wrote an AgentDefinition for each subagent, and the coordinator's prompt describes when to delegate. In testing, the coordinator never spawns a subagent and answers from its own knowledge. Its configuration includes allowedTools: ["Read", "Write"]. Which change should the team make?
opcoes: Add "Task" to the coordinator's allowedTools, since the Task tool is how a coordinator spawns subagents from their AgentDefinitions.
Strengthen the coordinator's system prompt so it states that each research question must be delegated to the relevant subagents.
Give the coordinator the subagents' tools directly, such as web search and document parsing, so it can complete the research steps itself.
Expose each subagent as a tool on its own MCP server, so the coordinator can call the subagents the same way it calls other tools.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, and a coordinator can use it only if its allowedTools includes "Task". Without it, no prompt wording lets the coordinator delegate, so it falls back to answering on its own.
feedbacks: Correct. The coordinator needs "Task" in allowedTools to spawn subagents.
The prompt already describes delegation; a prompt cannot grant access to a tool that is not allowed.
This turns the coordinator into a generalist with too many tools and loses the specialization and context isolation that subagents provide.
Wrapping subagents in MCP servers adds infrastructure to recreate what the Task tool already provides.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's analysts run long investigations with the research system from the Claude Code CLI. Each morning they start a new session and paste the previous day's report draft, but the agent loses its reasoning about which sources it had rejected and why, and spends the first hour re-reading them. The sources have not changed between days. What should the team change?
opcoes: Name each investigation's session and continue it the next day with --resume <session-name>, so the agent picks up that conversation and its context.
Use fork_session each morning on the previous day's session, so that the agent continues on a fresh branch while the earlier session stays unchanged.
Store the list of rejected sources and the reasons in the project CLAUDE.md, so that each new session the analysts start loads them automatically.
Paste the full source list and the raw notes along with the draft into each new session, so the agent has each input it used on the previous day.
questoes.explicacao: When prior context is still valid, resuming the named session with --resume <session-name> continues that specific conversation, including the reasoning that a pasted draft does not carry. Starting fresh with a summary is the better choice only when earlier tool results have gone stale, which is not the case here.
feedbacks: Correct. Named resumption continues the specific prior conversation with its valid context.
Forking creates a divergent branch from a shared baseline to explore alternatives; continuing one line of work is what resumption is for.
CLAUDE.md holds standing project instructions for everyone, not the working state of one investigation.
More pasted material helps, but it is still a reconstruction. Raw notes do not restore the agent's reasoning and still have to be reprocessed.

questoes.pergunta: Your pharmacy chain's document analysis subagent has a single tool, analyze_document(doc_id, instructions), which the coordinator uses to extract figures, summarize documents and check claims against sources. When asked to verify "the chain raised insulin copays by 12% in 2025" against a source, the tool often returns a general summary with no verdict, and the shape of its output differs from call to call. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The coordinator's request does not ask clearly enough for a verdict, so the analysis subagent defaults to summarizing the document it was given.
One generic tool with free-form instructions has no defined input/output contract for each purpose, so checks, extractions and summaries blur together.
The analysis subagent's context is crowded with earlier documents, so it loses track of which task each new call to analyze_document should perform.
The analysis subagent has no few-shot examples of verdict-style answers, so it writes a summary whenever a request matches no pattern it has seen.
questoes.explicacao: A generic analyze_document tool leaves its purpose to free-form instructions, so nothing fixes what a verification must return. Splitting it into purpose-specific tools, such as extract_figures, summarize_document and verify_claim_against_source, each with defined inputs and outputs, makes the verdict part of the contract.
feedbacks: Clearer requests may help some calls, but the output shape still varies because nothing defines what each kind of call returns.
Correct. Splitting the generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined contracts fixes the variation.
Nothing in the symptoms points to context load; the variation appears on any call, which points to the tool's contract.
Examples can shape the output, but they patch one symptom of a tool that has no defined contract for any of its purposes.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. You work at an online electronics retailer whose platform team builds developer productivity tools with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and the company's MCP servers; shared skills and CLAUDE.md files live in the repositories. The team shares a project skill, .claude/skills/scaffold-endpoint/SKILL.md, that generates boilerplate for new storefront API endpoints. An engineer wanted his scaffolds to also include load-test stubs, so he edited that SKILL.md in his checkout, and the change was merged with an unrelated pull request. Now every engineer's scaffolds include load-test stubs that most of them do not want. What was the flaw in how he customized the skill?
opcoes: He should have added context: fork to the skill's frontmatter, so the extra load-test output would stay isolated from his teammates' sessions.
He should have copied the skill to ~/.claude/skills/scaffold-endpoint/ under the same name, so his invocation stayed identical and the shared file stayed untouched.
He should have created a personal variant in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name, such as scaffold-endpoint-loadtest, leaving the shared skill unchanged.
He should have put the load-test instructions in his ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so they would apply only to his own sessions without touching the shared skill.
questoes.explicacao: Personal customizations belong in ~/.claude/skills/ as a variant with a different name, which leaves the shared project skill unchanged for teammates. Editing the project SKILL.md changed the behavior for everyone who pulls the repository.
feedbacks: context: fork isolates a skill's output from the main conversation; it does nothing to stop a change to a shared file from reaching other engineers.
Keeping it personal is right, but reusing the shared skill's name collides with the project skill and makes it unclear which one runs. A distinct name avoids that.
Correct. A personal variant with a different name in ~/.claude/skills/ customizes his workflow without affecting teammates.
CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so the load-test instructions would affect every task in his sessions, not just scaffolding. A personal skill is invoked on demand.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's engineers share a /gen-migration skill that needs a table name and a description of the change. Engineers often invoke it with no arguments; the skill then guesses a table from the open file and generates the wrong migration about a third of the time. Its SKILL.md frontmatter has a description and allowed-tools, nothing else. Which statement about fixing this is correct?
opcoes: Adding context: fork makes the skill run in a sub-agent that asks the engineer for any missing inputs before it starts, which prevents the guessing.
Adding argument-hint, such as "<table-name> <change-description>", prompts engineers for the required parameters when they invoke the skill without them.
Removing Read from allowed-tools stops the skill from inspecting the open file, which forces it to ask the engineer for the table name before it generates.
Declaring the required parameters in the project CLAUDE.md makes Claude check that they were supplied before it runs any skill, including this one.
questoes.explicacao: argument-hint frontmatter tells engineers which parameters a skill expects when they invoke it without arguments, which addresses the missing inputs at the source. context: fork only isolates the skill's output, and removing tools cripples the skill instead of collecting the parameters.
feedbacks: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context to keep its output out of the main conversation; it does not add a step that collects missing parameters.
Correct. argument-hint prompts developers for required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments.
This blocks one way of guessing but also stops the skill from reading files it legitimately needs, and nothing tells engineers what to provide.
CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded standards; it is not a parameter-validation mechanism for skills.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's engineers ask the agent to implement a PriceRoundingService for multi-currency checkout: banker's rounding for EUR, whole units for JPY, negative amounts for refunds, and 50,000 line items in under 200 ms. Three generated versions looked correct but failed edge cases found in QA. A teammate proposes describing the rules in more detail in the prompt and asking the agent to check its code against that description. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: a more detailed description plus a self-check against it is the lightest change, and the agent can catch the gaps the earlier prompts left open.
Adopt it with a second agent instance that reviews the code against the description, so the check is not made by the same session that wrote the code.
Reject it: let the agent implement the service first and then generate tests from that implementation, so that the tests match the code being deployed.
Reject it: write tests for the rules, the edge cases and the 200 ms limit first, then have the agent implement and iterate by sharing the failing tests.
questoes.explicacao: Test-driven iteration turns the requirements into executable checks: write a suite covering expected behavior, edge cases and the performance requirement, then let the agent iterate on concrete failures. Prose descriptions, even detailed ones, are interpreted inconsistently, and tests derived from the implementation would encode its bugs.
feedbacks: The prose was already interpreted inconsistently three times; a self-check against the same prose shares its gaps.
An independent reviewer helps catch subtle bugs, but it still checks against prose. Executable tests define the behavior precisely, including the 200 ms requirement.
Tests derived from the implementation encode whatever it does, bugs included. Tests should define the expected behavior before the implementation exists.
Correct. Write the test suite first, including edge cases and performance, then iterate by sharing failures.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's monorepo has a 1,900-line root CLAUDE.md covering testing, API conventions, deployment, accessibility and analytics events. Three teams edit it, merge conflicts are frequent and owners struggle to find their sections. The conventions must keep applying automatically in every session, and engineers do not want to change how they invoke the agent. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Turn each section into a project skill in .claude/skills/, so each team owns its own SKILL.md and engineers invoke the conventions they need for a task.
Move each team's sections into the ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md of that team's engineers, so each team edits its own copy without touching a shared file.
Split the content into CLAUDE.md files in the top-level directories, so each directory carries the conventions of the team that owns most of its code.
Split the content into topic files in .claude/rules/, such as testing.md, api-conventions.md and deployment.md, each maintained by its owning team.
questoes.explicacao: The .claude/rules/ directory organizes conventions into focused topic files as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md. Each team owns its file, which cuts merge conflicts, and the rules still load automatically, so nothing changes in how engineers invoke the agent.
feedbacks: Skills are on-demand, which breaks the requirement that the conventions apply automatically in every session.
User-level files are not shared through version control, so the conventions would reach only engineers who copy them and would drift between copies.
Testing, API and deployment conventions cut across directories, and a directory's CLAUDE.md applies only when Claude works in that directory.
Correct. Topic-specific rule files replace the monolith while keeping the conventions automatic.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent runs a dependency audit across 40 repositories: the coordinator spawns one subagent per repository, and each subagent queries the internal package-registry MCP server, which times out on about 3% of calls. Today a subagent returns "error" on its first timeout, and the coordinator re-spawns it, repeating all the work the subagent had already completed. Audits take 2.5 times longer than planned. Which TWO changes should you make? Choose TWO.
opcoes: When a subagent cannot resolve a failure, have it return the error type, what it attempted and the partial results it already collected.
Have each subagent retry registry timeouts locally, a bounded number of times with backoff, before it reports anything to the coordinator.
Route each registry call through the coordinator, so that timeouts and other errors are handled consistently in one central place.
Have a subagent return an empty package list for any repository whose registry calls time out, so that the audit still completes on schedule.
Have the coordinator re-spawn a failed subagent automatically up to three times before it marks that repository's audit as failed.
questoes.explicacao: Transient failures such as timeouts are best recovered locally inside the subagent, which avoids discarding completed work. Only failures the subagent cannot resolve should reach the coordinator, together with what was attempted and the partial results, so the coordinator can decide what to do without restarting everything.
feedbacks: Correct. Unresolvable failures go up with context and partial results, so the coordinator can decide what to do next.
Correct. Local recovery handles transient failures where they happen, without losing completed work.
Communication between agents should go through the coordinator, but routing every tool call there removes local recovery and makes the coordinator a bottleneck.
An empty list reported as success hides the failure and makes an unaudited repository look clean.
Re-spawning repeats all the completed work, which is exactly what makes the audits slow today.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent opens dependency-upgrade pull requests automatically. When an upgrade breaks something it cannot fix, it escalates to the owning team's on-call engineer through a ticket that currently reads "Upgrade of payments-sdk to 5.0 failed. See agent logs." On-call engineers have no access to the agent's session logs and spend about 40 minutes reconstructing each case. Which TWO elements should the escalation protocol require in the ticket? Choose TWO.
opcoes: A root-cause analysis citing the failing test or error, plus a recommended next action, such as pinning the version or migrating a call.
The agent's self-reported confidence that the problem can be fixed, so on-call engineers can triage the least promising cases first.
The commands the agent ran during the upgrade, in order, so that the engineer can replay the whole attempt locally if needed.
A link to the agent's full session transcript, so that the engineer can follow each step of the agent's reasoning about the upgrade.
The identifiers the engineer needs to act: repository, owning service, pull request, the package and the versions involved.
questoes.explicacao: A structured handoff gives the human what is needed to act without the transcript: the details that identify the case, a root-cause analysis and a recommended action. Links to logs the engineer cannot open, raw command histories and confidence scores do not replace a concise, structured summary.
feedbacks: Correct. Root cause and a recommended action are the core of a structured handoff.
Self-reported confidence is not a reliable signal of how hard a case is, and it does not tell the engineer what to do.
A raw command history is detailed but unstructured; the engineer still has to work out what went wrong and what to do.
The engineers cannot open session logs, and even with access a transcript makes them reconstruct the case themselves.
Correct. The handoff must identify the case so the engineer can act on it.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent triages flaky tests. When it concludes that a flaky test needs a human, it escalates to the owning team by pasting its last 30 messages into a ticket. Teams say they cannot act without asking follow-up questions, and the triage board cannot route or sort these tickets. The requirement is that an engineer who never saw the conversation can act on the ticket directly. What should you change?
opcoes: Attach the agent's complete conversation to the ticket instead of the last 30 messages, so that no part of the investigation is left out of the handoff.
Give on-call engineers access to the agent's sessions, so they can resume the triage session with --resume and ask their specific questions directly.
Have the agent write a short free-text summary of the investigation at the top of the ticket, followed by the 30 messages as supporting detail.
Have the agent compile a structured summary as ticket fields: test ID, owning service, root cause with evidence, fixes attempted and recommended action.
questoes.explicacao: Humans receiving an escalation usually lack the conversation, so the agent should compile a structured handoff summary with the facts needed to act: identifiers, root cause, what was tried and the recommended action. Structured fields also let the triage board route and sort tickets, which free text cannot do.
feedbacks: More transcript means more reading; the engineer still has to extract the root cause and the next step.
This shifts the reconstruction work onto the engineer and still depends on reading the conversation.
A summary beats raw messages, but free text can omit key facts and cannot be routed or sorted by the board.
Correct. A structured handoff summary lets someone without the transcript act, and its fields support routing.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent has two MCP tools with one-line descriptions: search_tickets ("Searches tickets") and search_incidents ("Searches incidents"). Logs show it passing free text to search_incidents, which accepts only incident IDs such as INC-204511 or ISO 8601 date ranges, and using search_tickets for questions about production outages. Which TWO changes would most improve how the agent selects and calls these tools? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Add a system prompt rule that sends any request mentioning "outage" or "down" to search_incidents, so outage questions stop reaching search_tickets.
State the boundary: outages and paging events go to search_incidents and work items to search_tickets, with a bug filed from an incident as an edge case.
Start both descriptions with "IMPORTANT: choose carefully between this tool and the other search tool", so the agent pays more attention.
In search_incidents, state the accepted input formats, INC- identifiers or ISO 8601 date ranges, and give an example query for each one.
Add to each description the name of the backing system and the team that owns it, so the agent knows where each tool's data comes from.
questoes.explicacao: Tool descriptions are the main input the model uses to choose and call tools. Stating the accepted input formats with examples fixes the malformed calls, and stating the boundary between similar tools, including edge cases, fixes the misrouting. Keyword rules in the system prompt create brittle associations that can override good descriptions.
feedbacks: Keyword-sensitive instructions create unintended associations ("the checkout page is down" may really be a bug ticket) and can override well-written descriptions.
Correct. Explicit boundaries and edge cases separate the two similar tools.
Emphasis does not give the model the information that distinguishes the tools.
Correct. Input formats with example queries prevent malformed calls.
Ownership details do not tell the model what inputs a tool accepts or when to choose it.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent generated a script that migrates customer addresses from a legacy schema. The script wrote the text "null" when apartment was NULL and dropped leading zeros from postal codes stored as integers. Over three rounds, the engineer replied "handle nulls and other edge cases properly"; each round fixed one case and broke another. What was the flaw in this iteration?
opcoes: The migration should have been planned in plan mode first, since a data migration between schemas is a multi-step change with architectural impact.
The agent should have received a full export of the legacy table, so that it could discover the edge cases in the real data on its own.
The feedback stayed general; it should have given test cases with example input rows and the exact expected output for each of them.
The engineer should have asked for defensive null checks on every column of the script instead of fixing the edge cases one at a time.
questoes.explicacao: When edge-case handling keeps regressing, specific test cases with example input and expected output (a NULL apartment becomes an empty field; postal code 2134 becomes "02134") show the agent exactly what correct means. A general instruction such as "handle nulls properly" is interpreted differently on each round.
feedbacks: Plan mode helps with design decisions, but the problem here is that the feedback in each round never pinned down the expected behavior.
A full export adds a lot of context but still does not say what the correct output is for each case.
