Correct. Concrete input/output test cases fix edge-case handling far more reliably than general instructions.
Blanket null checks do not define the expected output, and the postal code problem is not a null at all.

questoes.pergunta: Before deleting a legacy computeShippingFee function, an engineer asked your retailer's agent to find every caller. The agent ran Grep for computeShippingFee and reported four call sites. After the deletion, the build failed in 11 more places: shipping/index.ts re-exports the function as getDeliveryQuote, and utils/pricing.ts wraps it as estimateCartCharges. Which statement describes how the agent should have traced the usage?
opcoes: It should first identify every name under which the function is exported or wrapped, then run Grep for each of those names across the codebase.
It should use Glob to list the TypeScript files and then Read them all, since content search cannot follow a function through a re-export.
It should Grep with a broader pattern such as "Shipping|shipping", so that a single search catches the renamed exports and their callers.
It should delete the function and use Bash to run the compiler, since the build errors list each usage more reliably than any search.
questoes.explicacao: Wrapper modules and re-exports hide usages behind other names. The reliable approach is to identify all exported names first, by reading the module that exports the function and any wrappers, and then search for each name across the codebase.
feedbacks: Correct. Identify all exported and wrapped names first, then Grep for each of them.
Reading every file is slow and consumes context; Grep works well once you search for the right names.
Neither getDeliveryQuote nor estimateCartCharges contains "Shipping", so a broader pattern still misses them while adding noise.
The compiler reveals breakage only after the deletion; it is not a way to understand usage before making the change.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent generates onboarding guides by spawning one subagent per service across 12 services. When one subagent hits a permission error on a private submodule, the whole run aborts and nothing is produced. An engineer proposes catching the error in the subagent and returning an empty section marked as successful, so the run always completes. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: a guide with one empty section is more useful than no guide at all, and readers who notice the empty section can ask the owning team.
Reject it: the subagent should report a structured error with what it attempted and any partial results, and the coordinator should annotate the gap.
Accept it, but have the subagent also write a structured error entry to a server-side log, so engineers can investigate the permission problem later.
Reject it: keep aborting the run, but add automatic retries in the subagent, so permission errors have a chance to clear before the run stops.
questoes.explicacao: Returning an empty result as success silently suppresses the failure, and aborting the whole run on one failure discards the other 11 sections; both are anti-patterns. Structured error context lets the coordinator complete the guide and annotate the missing coverage.
feedbacks: This trades one anti-pattern for another: the coordinator is told the section succeeded, so nothing marks the gap.
Correct. Neither suppress the error nor abort everything: propagate structured context and annotate the gap.
A log helps operators, but the coordinator still receives a false success and the guide still hides the gap.
Permission errors are not transient, so retries waste time, and aborting the run still discards 11 good sections.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's team owns a deploy-info MCP server that returns {"isError": true, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Operation failed"}]} for every failure: a misspelled service name, the deploy API being unavailable or an engineer lacking production permissions. The agent retries three times in every case and then reports that the tool is broken. The team can change the server but cannot change the agent's system prompt this quarter. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Return error metadata (an errorCategory, an isRetryable flag, a readable description), so the agent can fix the input, retry or explain the permission issue.
Add retries with backoff inside the server and keep the generic message, so that transient outages are absorbed before the agent ever sees an error.
Return an empty successful result whenever a service name is not found, so that the agent stops retrying requests that can never succeed at all.
Split deploy-info into one tool per environment, so that failures in production are isolated from failures in the staging and test environments.
questoes.explicacao: A uniform "Operation failed" hides whether an error is a validation problem, a transient outage or a permission issue, so the agent cannot choose the right recovery. Structured metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable and a description) lets it correct the input, retry only what is retryable and explain permission problems, without any change to the prompt.
feedbacks: Correct. Structured error metadata gives the agent what it needs to choose the right recovery.
Server-side retries help with transient outages, but validation and permission failures would still arrive as the same generic message.
A misspelled name is an input error, not a valid empty result; reporting success hides the mistake from the agent and the engineer.
This changes how the tools are split, not what the agent learns from a failure.

questoes.pergunta: Your retailer's agent has a coordinator with four subagents: codebase explorer, dependency analyzer, test generator and documentation writer. It runs all four in sequence for every request, so a question such as "what does CartMerge do?" takes six minutes and returns tests and documentation nobody asked for. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add a keyword-based router in front of the coordinator that maps each type of request to a fixed subset of the four subagents.
Run the four subagents in parallel instead of in sequence, so the full pipeline finishes in about the time of its slowest subagent.
Have the coordinator analyze what each request needs and invoke only the relevant subagents, guided by a clear purpose for each.
Remove the test generator and the documentation writer from the coordinator and offer them as skills that engineers invoke explicitly.
questoes.explicacao: A coordinator should analyze each request's requirements and choose which subagents to invoke instead of routing everything through the full pipeline. A question about one function needs only the explorer. This is a change to the coordinator's prompt and design, not new infrastructure.
feedbacks: A keyword router is extra infrastructure that maps fixed subsets to keywords and breaks on requests nobody anticipated.
Parallelism shortens the wait but still produces tests and documentation nobody asked for.
Correct. The coordinator should select subagents dynamically based on what each request requires.
This pushes the routing decision onto engineers and removes capabilities the coordinator could use when a request needs them.

questoes.pergunta: A staff engineer at your retailer wrote precise instructions for the internal catalog-service API (pagination rules; never call write endpoints in production) in her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. The agent follows them in her runs, but her teammates' runs keep violating them. She is choosing between posting the snippet on the wiki for everyone to paste into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and moving it into the repository's CLAUDE.md. Which choice is better, and why?
opcoes: The repository's CLAUDE.md, because it is version-controlled and loads for everyone in the repository, while user-level files apply only to their owner.
The wiki, because each engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is loaded in each project they work on, so the rules would also be applied outside this repository.
Neither: a command in .claude/commands/ that loads the instructions is better, so that engineers bring in the rules only when they call the API.
The repository's CLAUDE.md, with a single @import line pointing to her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so she can keep maintaining the rules in one place.
questoes.explicacao: Instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply only to that user and are not shared through version control, which is why only her runs follow them. Putting them in the project CLAUDE.md shares them with every teammate automatically and keeps one reviewed source.
feedbacks: Correct. Project-level CLAUDE.md is shared through version control; user-level instructions are not.
Loading everywhere for each user is not the goal: the rules concern this repository, and copies pasted by hand drift and are easily skipped.
Commands are on-demand; a rule such as never calling production write endpoints must apply even when nobody remembers to load it.
The import would point to a file that exists only on her machine, so her teammates would still not receive the instructions.

questoes.pergunta: For "explain this legacy module" requests, your retailer's coordinator spawns three independent subagents: one traces callers, one summarizes the data model and one lists configuration flags. Each takes about 2.5 minutes. Logs show one Task call per coordinator turn, each started after the previous one returns, so requests take about eight minutes. The requirement is under three minutes. What should you change?
opcoes: Merge the three subagents into one subagent that performs all three investigations, so that the coordinator makes a single Task call per request.
Lower each subagent's max_tokens so that each finishes sooner, keeping the three sequential Task calls but cutting the time each one takes.
Have the coordinator emit all three Task calls in a single response, so that the three subagents run in parallel rather than one after another.
Have each subagent spawn the next one when it finishes, so the coordinator no longer waits between turns before it starts another subagent.
questoes.explicacao: Independent subagents run in parallel when the coordinator emits multiple Task tool calls in the same response. Sequential calls across separate turns add up their durations; parallel calls bring the total close to the slowest subagent.
feedbacks: One subagent doing all three tasks still runs them in sequence and loses the focus of separate contexts.
Shorter outputs degrade the results and still leave three sequential runs.
Correct. Multiple Task calls in one coordinator response spawn the subagents in parallel.
Chaining subagents keeps the work sequential and takes control of the flow away from the coordinator.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. You work at a regional bank that built a structured data extraction system with Claude. It extracts information from unstructured loan documents such as pay stubs, bank statements, appraisals and tax returns, validates the output against JSON schemas and feeds the loan origination system, so it must stay highly accurate and handle edge cases gracefully. The pipeline asks the model for one confidence score per document and sends documents scoring below 0.8 to human review; the team picked 0.8 because it sounded reasonable. After three months, 88% of reviewed documents needed no correction, while an audit found that 6% of auto-approved debt_to_income values were wrong, many from documents scored 0.9 or higher. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: Self-reported confidence carries no information about extraction quality, so the routing has no usable signal and each document should go to human review.
The 0.8 threshold is too low for lending data; raising it to 0.95 would send the uncertain debt_to_income extractions to review and let the rest through.
Routing relies on one document-level score with a guessed threshold, instead of field-level scores with thresholds set from a labeled validation set.
Reviewers approve routed documents too quickly; adding a second reviewer to each routed document would catch the errors the first one misses.
questoes.explicacao: A single document-level score hides which fields are at risk, and a threshold chosen without labeled data has no known relation to actual error rates. Field-level confidence scores with thresholds calibrated on a labeled validation set let the team route review attention to fields such as debt_to_income, where the scores actually predict errors.
feedbacks: Confidence becomes useful once it is field-level and calibrated against labeled data; sending every document to review ignores reviewer capacity.
A higher threshold is still uncalibrated and still document-level, so it may flood review without targeting the fields that fail.
Correct. Field-level confidence, calibrated on a labeled validation set, is what makes confidence-based routing reliable.
The wrong values are in documents that never reach reviewers; more reviewers do not change what gets routed.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank moved two extraction workflows to the Message Batches API for its 50% savings: a weekly portfolio audit that is submitted on Friday evening and due on Monday morning, and the extraction behind the branch "instant pre-approval" screen, where a loan officer waits with the customer. Since the change, officers report waits from 20 minutes to several hours. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The pre-approval requests are sent without custom_id values, so results cannot be matched to the waiting officers' sessions until the entire batch ends.
The pre-approval batches are submitted too rarely; submitting a new batch every five minutes would guarantee each officer a wait of a few minutes.
Pre-approval blocks a waiting officer and batches have no latency guarantee, so it needs the synchronous API, while the weekly audit can stay on batch.
Both workflows belong on the synchronous API, because a processing window of up to 24 hours is too risky even for an audit due the following Monday.
questoes.explicacao: Batch processing suits latency-tolerant, non-blocking work such as a weekly audit with a weekend of slack, but it has no guaranteed latency and can take up to 24 hours. A workflow in which a person is waiting is blocking, so it needs the synchronous API.
feedbacks: custom_id correlates requests with results, but it does not change how long a batch takes to process.
Submitting more often does not help: each batch still has no latency guarantee.
Correct. Blocking workflows need the synchronous API; latency-tolerant ones can use batch.
Friday evening to Monday morning is longer than the 24-hour window, so the audit is a good fit for the batch savings.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's pipeline includes a step that flags issues in extracted commercial lease abstracts for credit analysts. Its prompt says "flag anything unusual in the lease terms". Analysts report that 70% of flags are standard clauses, such as common area maintenance charges and ordinary renewal options, and they have started skimming past the flags. Which TWO changes would most improve precision? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Send the flags to an independent model instance that removes any flag it considers standard, so analysts receive only flags both instances accept.
Have the model rate each flag from 1 to 10 and show analysts only the flags rated 8 or higher, so low-value flags are filtered out automatically.
List the clause types to skip, such as standard maintenance charges and ordinary renewal options, unless a specific stated condition applies.
Add an explicit instruction to flag only findings the model is highly confident about, so that borderline clauses no longer reach the analysts.
Replace "anything unusual" with explicit conditions to flag, such as a lease term ending before loan maturity or a tenant termination right within the loan term.
questoes.explicacao: Vague instructions like "anything unusual" leave the model to guess, so it flags whatever looks different. Explicit criteria that define what to report and what to skip improve precision; confidence-based filters and a second instance applying the same vague standard do not.
feedbacks: A second instance with the same vague standard adds cost without defining what is unusual.
Confidence-based filtering keeps the vague criterion and hides some flags without defining which ones matter.
Correct. Stating what to skip, and when, removes the standard clauses from the flags.
General instructions such as "only high-confidence findings" do not improve precision; the model still lacks a definition of what matters.
Correct. Explicit, categorical conditions define what is worth reporting.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's small-business loan schema declares co_signer_name and co_signer_income as required fields. About 30% of applications have no co-signer, and an audit found invented but plausible co-signer details in 4% of those extractions. An engineer proposes making both fields nullable and instructing the model to return null when the application contains no co-signer. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: required fields push the model to produce a value even when none exists, and a nullable field gives it a valid way to represent absence.
Reject it: keep both fields required and add an instruction never to invent values, since the schema should stay strict for downstream systems.
Reject it: keep the fields required and have the model return the string "N/A" when there is no co-signer, so downstream code always gets a value.
Adopt it, and add a retry with error feedback whenever either field comes back null, so that co-signers the model missed are caught on retry.
questoes.explicacao: When source documents may not contain a value, required fields pressure the model to fabricate one. Making the fields optional or nullable removes that pressure and lets absence be represented explicitly.
feedbacks: Correct. Nullable fields prevent fabrication when the information is absent from the source.
The instruction fights the schema: the schema still demands a value, so fabrication remains likely.
A sentinel string looks like data to downstream systems and keeps the field required; null states absence unambiguously.
Retrying cannot produce a co-signer who does not exist; null is the correct result for 30% of applications.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank extracts income data from about 6,000 mortgage documents a day, and the review team can check 400. Today a random 7% of documents go to review: reviewers find nothing to correct in most of them, while audits keep finding errors in files they never saw. The model already outputs field-level confidence scores calibrated on a labeled set, and many applications include both a pay stub and a W-2. Reviewer capacity cannot grow. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Keep random selection but raise it to fill all 400 daily slots, so that the share of documents checked rises while the sample stays unbiased.
Fill all 400 slots with the largest loan amounts and first-time applicants first, since those files carry the most financial risk for the bank.
Send files whose sources contradict each other back to the applicant, and fill the 400 slots with the lowest document-level confidence scores.
Fill all 400 slots by priority: extractions with low field-level confidence and files with contradictory or ambiguous sources first.
questoes.explicacao: With fixed capacity, review should go where errors are most likely: low-confidence extractions and documents whose sources are ambiguous or contradictory. Random selection is useful for measuring error rates, but as the only routing rule it spends scarce reviewer time on documents that were extracted correctly.
feedbacks: Random sampling measures error rates, but as the routing rule it spends most of the capacity on correct extractions.
Loan size and applicant history measure the bank's financial exposure, not the likelihood that an extraction is wrong; review capacity should go where extraction errors are likely.
Contradictory sources are exactly what reviewers should see; pushing them back to applicants delays loans, and a document-level score hides which fields are uncertain.
Correct. Limited reviewer capacity should be prioritized toward low-confidence and contradictory cases.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's pipeline checks extracted bank statements for inconsistencies with the applicant's stated income. The prompt already lists explicit criteria, yet 35% of flags are dismissed, and the dismissed cases vary from week to week: payroll split across two deposits, tax refunds, transfers between the applicant's own accounts. What is the most effective first step to reduce these false positives?
opcoes: Add few-shot examples that pair acceptable patterns, such as split payroll, with genuine issues, each explaining why it is or is not a problem.
Keep an exclusion list of the benign transaction descriptions seen so far and extend it weekly, so those exact patterns are no longer flagged.
Add an instruction to flag only the inconsistencies the model is highly confident about, so that borderline cases such as split deposits drop out.
Train a classifier on the past year of dismissed flags and run it after the model, so that flags resembling earlier dismissals are filtered out.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot examples that contrast acceptable patterns with genuine issues, and explain the reasoning, let the model generalize to benign patterns it has not seen before. An exclusion list only covers patterns already seen, and here the false positives change every week.
feedbacks: Correct. Contrasting examples with reasoning reduce false positives and generalize to new benign patterns.
An exclusion list matches only the cases already seen; next week's new benign pattern will still be flagged.
Confidence instructions do not tell the model what is acceptable, and they tend to suppress true issues along with false ones.
A trained classifier is heavy infrastructure for a problem that targeted examples in the prompt should address first.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's validation rejects 9% of commercial loan packages because guarantor_net_worth is missing. Investigation shows that in these packages the figure appears only in a personal financial statement that applicants submit separately, after the package has been extracted. The team is choosing a design for handling these failures. Which should it adopt?
opcoes: Retry the extraction with error feedback naming the missing field, up to three times, since specific feedback usually lets the model correct its output.
Record guarantor_net_worth as null with a reason such as "not in submitted documents", and trigger a request for the personal financial statement.
Retry the extraction with a larger model on the same documents, since a stronger model is more likely to find a figure that the first one missed.
Retry once, and if the field is still missing, have the model estimate net worth from the guarantor's income and the assets listed in the package.
questoes.explicacao: Retry with error feedback works for format and structural errors, but it cannot recover information that is simply not in the source. Recording the absence explicitly and requesting the missing document addresses the real cause.
feedbacks: Feedback helps when the information is in the document; no number of retries finds a figure that lives in a document that was not provided.
Correct. Retries are ineffective for absent information; record the absence and obtain the missing source.
A larger model reads the same documents, and the figure is not in them.
An estimate presented as an extracted value is a fabrication that downstream lending decisions would rely on.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank extracts property_area_sqft and lot_size from appraisals and broker listings, where values appear as "approx. 2.4k sq ft", "0.3 ac", "about 1/4 acre" or "see sketch, p. 7". In 5% of extractions the model returns precise values that the document does not support, such as a lot size taken from a sketch reference. The requirement is to cut these hallucinated values without adding manual review. What should you change?
opcoes: Add few-shot examples of informal measurements in varied formats, such as "0.3 ac" becoming 13,068 sq ft and "see sketch" becoming null with a note.
Add an instruction to extract only values written as exact numbers and never to estimate, convert or infer a measurement from the wording.
Make lot_size a required number with minimum and maximum bounds in the schema, so implausible values are rejected and a valid figure is returned.
Run each extraction twice and keep a value only when both runs agree, so that values the model invents on a single run are dropped automatically.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot examples are effective at reducing hallucination in extraction tasks with informal measurements and varied document structures: they show which wording can be converted and which wording means the value is absent. Instructions alone are applied inconsistently, and voting does not catch values the model invents the same way each time.
feedbacks: Correct. Examples of informal measurements show the model how to normalize them and when to return null.
This also discards legitimate conversions such as "0.3 ac", and bare instructions handle varied wording inconsistently.
A required number increases the pressure to fabricate, and bounds accept any plausible invented value.
A model that misreads a sketch reference often misreads it the same way twice; agreement is not support in the document.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's system assembles a credit memo from extracted data: three years of financial ratios, recent news about the borrower and covenant compliance results. The memo template asks for "a concise bulleted summary in every section, for consistency". Credit officers say the ratio trends are hard to compare across years and the news items lose their context. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The extraction schemas round the financial ratios, so the memo cannot show the year-to-year differences that the credit officers need to compare.
The memo is too long for officers to read quickly, so it should be condensed further to keep only the most important figures and headlines.
The template forces one uniform format on all content, instead of tables for financials, prose for news and structured lists for compliance results.
The model has no example memos to follow, and without few-shot examples of a structured memo it falls back to bullets that flatten everything.
questoes.explicacao: Different content types read best in different forms: financial data as tables, news as prose and technical or compliance findings as structured lists. A template that forces every section into one format loses the comparability of the figures and the context of the news.
feedbacks: Nothing indicates lost precision; officers can see the values but cannot compare them easily as bullets.
Condensing further would make both problems worse; the issue is format, not length.
Correct. Each content type should be rendered in the form that suits it rather than one uniform format.
Examples could help, but the template explicitly requires bullets everywhere, so examples would conflict with it rather than fix it.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's extraction QA step flags five issue categories for loan processors: arithmetic mismatches, missing signatures, date inconsistencies, name mismatches and "suspicious formatting". Processors have started ignoring all flags. Data shows that suspicious-formatting flags are 82% false positives and make up 60% of all flags, while the other categories run at 5–15%. Which TWO actions should the team take? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Disable every flag category until the false-positive problem is solved, so processors are not trained to ignore flags in the meantime.
Keep each category active but attach a confidence score to each flag, so processors can sort the queue and look at the likeliest issues first.
Keep suspicious-formatting flags but lower their severity to informational, so they stay visible without interrupting the processors.
Rewrite the suspicious-formatting criteria with concrete definitions and examples, and test them on past dismissed flags before re-enabling.
Temporarily disable the suspicious-formatting category, so processors see only the accurate categories while their trust in the flags recovers.
questoes.explicacao: High false-positive categories undermine trust in the accurate ones. Temporarily disabling the noisy category restores trust in the remaining flags, while the team improves that category's prompt with explicit criteria and checks it against past dismissals before turning it back on.
feedbacks: The other four categories are accurate; disabling them throws away useful signal.
Sorting by confidence keeps the noise in the queue and relies on confidence filtering instead of better criteria.
Informational flags are still noise in the same queue, and the criteria that produce them are unchanged.
Correct. Improve the noisy category's criteria and validate them before re-enabling it.
Correct. Temporarily disabling the noisy category restores trust in the accurate ones.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's pipeline currently prompts "Return the extracted fields as JSON" and parses the text of the reply. About 2.3% of replies fail to parse, because of commentary after the JSON or unescaped quotes inside addresses. The team plans to define an extraction tool whose input_schema is the target schema and to read the data from the tool_use block. Which statement about this change is correct?
opcoes: The parse failures come from the OCR text itself, so escaping the quotes in each source document before extraction would remove them just as reliably.
Reading the fields from the tool_use input removes these syntax failures, though checks such as totals matching their line items are still needed.
Adding "respond with valid JSON only, no commentary" and a sample object to the prompt would remove the failures without introducing any tools.
Tool use with a JSON schema removes both syntax and semantic errors, so the downstream checks on totals and dates can be retired after the change.
questoes.explicacao: Defining the extraction as a tool with a JSON schema and reading the structured input from the tool_use response eliminates JSON syntax errors. It does not prevent semantic errors, such as line items that do not sum to the stated total, so semantic validation stays.
feedbacks: Pre-escaping addresses one cause, but commentary after the JSON and other syntax problems remain.
Correct. Tool use with a schema eliminates syntax errors; semantic validation is still required.
Prompt instructions reduce the failure rate but do not guarantee schema-compliant output; tool use does.
This overstates the guarantee: the schema governs structure, not whether values are correct or consistent.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank's extraction system uses a coordinator with three subagents: a classifier that identifies the document type, an extractor and a validator. To simplify configuration, an engineer proposes giving all three subagents the same 14 tools, including write_to_core_banking, fetch_credit_report and send_customer_email. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it: each subagent's system prompt says which tools fit its role, so the extra tools will simply go unused while configuration stays simple.
Accept it, adding a PreToolUse hook that blocks write_to_core_banking for the classifier and validator, so the riskiest misuse is stopped.
Reject it: give the subagents no tools and have the coordinator make each tool call on their behalf, so that access is controlled centrally.
Reject it: give each subagent only the tools its role needs, such as read-only checks for the validator, since broad tool sets invite misuse.
questoes.explicacao: Each subagent should have only the tools relevant to its role. Fourteen tools per agent increase decision complexity and degrade tool selection, and tools outside an agent's specialization tend to be misused, for example a validator writing to core banking.
feedbacks: Prompts guide but do not guarantee, and unused tools still add decision complexity and room for misuse.
A hook can stop one dangerous call, but every subagent still chooses among 14 tools, which degrades selection and leaves other misuse possible.
Centralizing every tool call overloads the coordinator and leaves the subagents unable to do their work.
Correct. Scope each subagent's tools to its role to prevent cross-specialization misuse.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank moved its nightly statement extraction to the Message Batches API. Each request lets the model call lookup_branch_code and get_fx_rate during extraction. Every document that needed a lookup came back ending in a tool_use block, with no extraction. The team wants to keep the batch savings for this nightly volume. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Raise max_tokens on each batch request, so that the model has room to finish both the lookups and the extraction within the same request.
Resolve branch codes and the day's FX rates before submission and include them in each request, so every request completes without a tool call.
Move the nightly extraction to the synchronous API, so the application can execute the tool calls and return their results to the model.
Set tool_choice to "any" in each batch request, so that the batch service itself executes the requested tool calls before it returns the result.
questoes.explicacao: The batch API cannot execute tools mid-request and return their results to the model, so a request that needs a tool stops at the tool_use block. Providing the lookup data up front lets each request complete in a single turn and keeps the batch discount.
feedbacks: The request did not run out of tokens; it stopped because it asked for a tool that nothing inside the batch can execute.
Correct. Batch requests cannot do multi-turn tool calling, so the data must be supplied up front.
This works technically but gives up the 50% savings the team wants to keep.
tool_choice controls whether the model calls a tool, not who executes it; nothing executes tools inside a batch request.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank builds a borrower profile by extracting facts from tax returns, audited financials and an appraisal, then condensing them into a summary for the credit system, which must trace every value to a document and page. After condensation, 30% of values have no traceable source, and when two documents report different revenue, the summary shows only one figure. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Append a list of every document used to the end of the profile, so that the credit system can see which sources contributed to the summary.
After the profile is written, have a separate model search the documents for each value and attach the best matching source to it.
Have every extraction output claim-source mappings (value, document, page, excerpt) that the condensing step must preserve and merge.
Instruct the condensing step to cite a source for each value it includes, and to choose the most recent figure when documents disagree.
questoes.explicacao: Attribution is lost when findings are compressed without claim-source mappings. Requiring structured mappings at extraction, and making the condensing step preserve and merge them, keeps every value traceable and lets conflicting figures appear side by side with their sources instead of one being chosen.
feedbacks: A document list does not say which value came from which page.
Re-attaching sources afterward is guesswork and can attach the wrong document to a value.
Correct. Structured claim-source mappings, preserved through condensation, keep provenance intact.
Instructions to cite help, but without structured mappings the condensing step still loses them, and picking the most recent figure discards a conflict that should be annotated.

questoes.pergunta: Your bank reviewed last week's validation failures: 140 statements where statement_period_end came back as "March 31st, 2026" instead of an ISO date, 60 where line items did not add up to the stated balance because a page was missing from the scan, and 35 where the account holder's name landed in bank_name. The team is deciding where to apply retry with error feedback. Which design should it adopt?
opcoes: Retry all three groups with specific error feedback, since telling the model exactly which check failed lets it correct its own extraction.
Retry none of them and send all three groups to human review, since a model that made an error once is likely to repeat it on a retry.
Retry only the 60 balance mismatches, since recomputing totals is something the model can do reliably once the mismatch is pointed out.
Retry the date-format and wrong-field groups with error feedback, and send the missing-page statements for a re-scan instead.
questoes.explicacao: Retries with specific error feedback work well for format mismatches and structural output errors, such as a date in the wrong format or a value in the wrong field. They cannot help when the information is not in the source, as with a missing page, which needs a new scan.
feedbacks: Feedback cannot recover line items from a page that was never scanned.
Format and field-placement errors are exactly the cases that retry with feedback fixes cheaply.
This is backwards: the totals cannot be fixed because data is missing, while the other two groups are fixable.
Correct. Retry where the information is present but badly formatted or placed; obtain the missing source otherwise.
